package_info.package_manager: Windows (malware distributed via PDF/MSI/DLL/EXE, not a traditional package manager)
package_info.why_malicious: CHAVECLOAK is a banking trojan that leverages malicious PDFs, MSI installers, DLL sideloading, and deceptive pop-ups to steal sensitive financial information from users, primarily targeting Brazil. It establishes persistence, exfiltrates credentials, manipulates user sessions, and enables remote control of the victim's device, resulting in financial theft and system compromise.

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: Upon user interaction (clicking the embedded link in the PDF), the code initiates a network request to download a ZIP archive containing the next-stage malware, resulting in the delivery of a malicious payload to the victim's system.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Embedding hidden links in PDFs that download executable archives from untrusted sources is a common malware delivery tactic.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate PDFs do not initiate downloads of executables or archives without explicit user intent and clear warning.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some business workflows use PDFs with download links, but these typically point to documents or trusted resources, not executables or archives.
key_indicators: Obfuscated or non-standard URL in PDF
Link initiates download of ZIP archive containing malware
No user warning or context for executable download

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: MSI drops Lightshot.exe and Lightshot.dll to %AppData%\Skillbrains\lightshot\5.5.0.7 and executes Lightshot.exe
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: During installation (MSI execution), the code writes both a legitimate executable (Lightshot.exe) and a malicious DLL (Lightshot.dll) to the AppData directory, then executes Lightshot.exe, which loads the malicious DLL via DLL sideloading, resulting in the execution of attacker-controlled code.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Dropping and executing files in AppData, especially with DLL sideloading, is a well-known malware persistence and evasion technique.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate installers should not sideload malicious DLLs or place executables in user AppData without clear justification.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some software uses DLL sideloading for plugin architectures, but not to execute hidden or malicious code.
key_indicators: Recent modification date on dropped DLL

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: GetVolumeInformationW; create %AppData%\[HEX ID]lIG.log; add registry key HKCU\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run\Lightshot; send HTTP request to hxxp://64[.]225[.]32[.]24/shn/inspecionando.php
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime (when Lightshot.exe loads the DLL), the code collects system information using GetVolumeInformationW, creates a log file in AppData, establishes persistence by adding a Run key in the registry, and sends a beacon containing system data to a remote C2 server, enabling ongoing attacker access.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Establishing persistence via registry and communicating with a C2 server are classic behaviors of malware seeking long-term control and data exfiltration.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate DLLs should not create persistence mechanisms or communicate with external servers without user consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate software may create log files or use registry Run keys, but not in conjunction with C2 beaconing or without transparency.
key_indicators: Log file creation in AppData with suspicious naming

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Periodically call GetForegroundWindow and GetWindowTextW; if window matches bank list, communicate with C2 and enable credential theft features (screen block, keylogging, pop-ups)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime (after passing geo-location checks), the code periodically monitors the active window using GetForegroundWindow and GetWindowTextW; if the window title matches a list of targeted banks, it communicates with the C2 server and activates credential theft features such as screen blocking, keylogging, and deceptive pop-ups, resulting in theft of sensitive user data.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Monitoring window titles for banking activity and enabling credential theft features is a hallmark of banking trojans.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software should not monitor window titles for banking activity or enable credential theft mechanisms.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some accessibility or parental control software may monitor windows, but not for the purpose of credential theft or C2-controlled actions.
key_indicators: Banking window detection via window title matching
Activation of keylogging and screen blocking

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: POST stolen credentials and system info to hxxp://comunidadebet20102[.]hopto[.]org/04/M/ (for Mercado Bitcoin) or other C2 paths
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime (after credentials are stolen), the code sends a HTTP POST request containing stolen credentials and system information to a remote C2 server, resulting in exfiltration of sensitive data to the attacker.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Exfiltrating credentials and system information to remote servers is a primary indicator of credential-stealing malware.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software should never transmit sensitive user credentials to unknown or untrusted servers.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some enterprise tools may send system info to trusted servers for support, but never user credentials or to suspicious domains.
key_indicators: HTTP POST requests to suspicious or hardcoded domains
Sensitive data (credentials, system info) in network payload

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: During installation (older variant), the code executes a PowerShell command to add its own directory to Windows Defender exclusions, preventing detection and removal by Windows Defender and enabling the malware to persist undetected.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Altering Windows Defender exclusions via PowerShell is a known malware evasion technique to avoid detection.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate installers should not modify antivirus exclusions for their own folders without clear, user-acknowledged justification.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some enterprise software may request exclusions, but this is always documented and user-approved, not hidden.

attack_chain.action: User opens malicious PDF and clicks embedded link, downloading ZIP archive.
attack_chain.leads_to: ZIP file is decompressed, MSI installer is executed.

attack_chain.action: MSI installer drops legitimate executable and malicious DLL, then executes the legitimate file to trigger DLL sideloading.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious DLL is loaded and executed.

attack_chain.action: Malicious DLL collects system info, creates log, establishes persistence, and beacons to C2.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malware is now persistent and ready to monitor user activity.

attack_chain.action: Malware monitors foreground windows for banking activity, then enables credential theft and remote control features.
attack_chain.leads_to: Credentials and sensitive data are stolen.

attack_chain.action: Stolen credentials and system info are exfiltrated to C2 servers.
Older variant: Adds malware directory to Windows Defender exclusions to evade detection.

behavioral_signatures: PDFs with embedded links to ZIP, MSI, or DLL payloads hosted on untrusted domains
MSI installers that drop DLLs with recent modification dates into AppData subdirectories
DLL sideloading via execution of legitimate executables in AppData
Creation of registry Run keys for unknown or suspicious executables
Foreground window monitoring for banking-related keywords or window titles
Activation of keylogging and screen blocking features triggered by banking window detection
HTTP POST exfiltration of credentials and system info to suspicious or hardcoded C2 domains
PowerShell commands that add malware directories to Windows Defender exclusions
file_indicators: Delphi executables with embedded payloads in RCData section
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for PDFs containing embedded links to executable downloads, especially ZIP, MSI, or DLL files hosted on untrusted domains. Detect MSI installers that drop DLLs with recent modification dates into AppData subdirectories and observe for DLL sideloading activity via legitimate executables. Flag creation of registry Run keys for unknown executables, foreground window monitoring for banking-related keywords, and PowerShell commands that add malware directories to Windows Defender exclusions. Correlate HTTP POST requests to known C2 domains and exfiltration endpoints with these behaviors for high-confidence detection of CHAVECLOAK and similar banking trojans.
